event: A new, never cycled HLB (SN 2-4943, kit HLBCK-413) was found on the battery checker with cell 6 at 2.78V while the other cells read 3.3 to 3.4V; no flight was involved.
failure_mode: single cell low voltage (self-discharge) in storage before first use
contributing: sibling HLB SN 2-4867 from the same kit HLBCK-413 and same date of manufacture 25-04-02 also had cell 6 low (2.95V), on VXEP-1492

evidence.quote: VXE30 Hybrid Lift Battery (HLB) SN 2-4943 DOM 25-04-02 from HLBCK-413 has cell 6 at 2.78V remaining cells 3.3-3.4V per HLB battery checker
No battery cycles, pulled straight from production HLB kit
Cell 6 shows 2.95V, other cells 3.3-3.4V using HLB battery checker

would_settle_it.what: Self-discharge, internal resistance and teardown of cell 6 of HLB SN 2-4943 (quarantined in the engineering fire cabinet) to find why the cell drained
Whether the systemic HLB cell finding (electrolyte loss, seal defects in the vendor cells) applies to this production lot

reasoning: The battery checker measurement shows one cell (cell 6) about 0.5V below the rest on a pack with no cycles, so the fault is a single low cell in the HLB. A second pack from the same kit and the same manufacture date also has cell 6 low, which points to a lot or pack assembly issue, but no teardown or test of the cell is recorded, so the mechanism is not known.
notes: No investigation recorded; ticket still New. The matching cell number and lot on VXEP-1492 suggests a common production cause but this is inference only.

event: VXE-575 (TIQUILA) MCM would not accept a customer OGCS update; on RMA it took OGCS 1.3.0 with no troubleshooting.
failure_mode: OGCS update to the MCM failed at the customer site

evidence.quote: VXE575 MCM will not accept OGCS update.
Failed to take MCM/OGCS Update to 1.1.1.
This aircraft was updated to OGCS 1.3.0 and the update went as expected with no troubleshooting required.
Not sure what may have caused the error on customer update to OGCS 1.2

would_settle_it.what: Screenshot added at closure, may show the update error or the successful version
The error message and MCM log from the failed customer update attempt

event: During flight tests of the E140Z G2 regulated payload cable on VXE 734 and 881, gimbal 6421 would not connect through Epsilon at boot (bad video packets) until AUX 1 power was cycled or an older Epsilon version was used; gimbal 6084 worked on both aircraft.
component: E140ZG2 gimbal SN 6421 with G2 regulated payload cable and Epsilon GUI
failure_mode: gimbal network link not established at boot (bad packets, no Epsilon connection) though the gimbal answered ping
contributing: Epsilon GUI version: gimbal 6421 on 734 only connected with Epsilon 3.5.5, not 13 or 14
bad video packets at boot on every aircraft and gimbal combination
VXEP-1452: new regulated cable network issues, suspected capacitor isolation without magnetics
separate GCS issue found: dual SA media client v3.3.10 blocked camera connection on one GCS

evidence.quote: We started by testing aircraft #734 with gimbal #6084 and quickly got the aircraft in the air with a good functional checkout and clean video
During boot-up we noticed bad packet appearing in the XCOMM throughput webpage and was unable to get the gimbal to connect through Epsilon.
After this hard reset the gimbal would not connect through Epsilon ver 14 or 13. We luckily still had ver 3.5.5 on the laptop and was able to connect without any issues
Here is the problematic capacitor isolation that is a likley cause/contributor to this issue and many others.

would_settle_it.what: Gimbal, cable and GCS serials and firmware per test, to separate the gimbal 6421 fault from the Epsilon version and cable
Bench test gimbal 6421 against 6084 on the same cable and Epsilon versions, with network diagnostics on the payload Ethernet link

reasoning: The swap tests show gimbal 6084 connected cleanly on both aircraft while gimbal 6421 failed to connect on both, so the problem follows gimbal 6421 or its pairing with the cable. Recovery by power cycling AUX 1 or by going back to Epsilon 3.5.5 means the Epsilon software version also plays a part, and the linked cable investigation suspects the new regulated cable network interface, so it cannot be pinned to one part.
notes: Two aircraft and two gimbals in one test write up; tests 3 and 4 are the failures. The ticket is a test report, not a single field incident.

event: VXE-559 (fuel cell configuration, 3rd SFG) made a strange motor noise during VTOL launch and was aborted below transition altitude; after landing the HLB popped and smoked, damaging the center wing, fuel tank and regulator.
failure_mode: HLB cell voltage dropout under VTOL lift load, then venting and smoking after landing
contributing: aircraft believed not flown since return from Alabama (long storage)
motors did not cut off automatically after landing and had to be disabled manually
aircraft never reached transition altitude (about 200 ft AGL at most), so the lack of transition is not a separate fault
radio failed bench test after the event (likely damage); fuel cell D4500530 repaired under RMA-798

evidence.quote: Ground Crew noticed a “weird sound” on the VTOL motors and called to abort the launch
Quick review confirms the relationship between this issue and the HLB voltage dropout investigation.
It never reached the transition altitude despite the operator statement. At most it was at 200 ft AGL.
fuel cell repaired in AA, HLB failure upon transistion, closing since HLB issue is tracked in systemic
Avionics box bench tested and working as designed
Battery Dissection led to discovery of leaking / evaporating electrolyte material inside the 3300mAh Advanced Energy Cells within the HLB.

team_view_in_comments: fuel cell repaired in AA, HLB failure upon transistion, closing since HLB issue is tracked in systemic

would_settle_it.what: Plot from the quick data review that ties this flight to the HLB cell voltage dropout
HLB cell voltages and lift motor commands during the launch and abort
Systemic 8D findings and whether HLB 3083 was dissected

reasoning: The engineer review of the data links this event to the systemic HLB cell voltage dropout, and the HLB is the part that vented after landing. Avionics bench tested good and the transition question was resolved as the aircraft never reached transition altitude. No teardown of this HLB is recorded, so the battery is the system but the cell level mechanism rests on the systemic investigation, not on this pack.
notes: Root Cause field is empty; the closing comment defers to systemic VXEP-1449, whose own root cause is the cell electrolyte loss finding. HLB SN 3083 comes from the VXEP-1449 tracking table. All images and AAR packs are listed only.

event: On a MARSOC VXE-30 Advanced Nav aircraft the MOD payload MAIM showed AHRS state X and its TI programmer would not connect for a firmware update; Trickster was not getting usable INS data.
failure_mode: MAIM running outdated firmware/GUI not set up for the Advanced Nav INS feed
contributing: Advanced Nav aircraft sends a different INS stream than the Eclipse AHRS the MAIM normally expects
update attempt from the GCS laptop failed at TI programmer connect; later succeeded on the Trickster laptop

evidence.quote: Customer did not have correct firmware/GUI. Seem concerned that upgrading will cause issues:
I recommend upgrading to the latest firmware/GUI whether or not you are using advanced nav. Firmware, detects if a AHRS is present and configures itself accordingly
So we got the maim to update from v30000 to v30001 on the Trickster laptop.
The maim AHRS is state is an X.

team_root_cause: No root cause identified, however leaning towards a software issue

would_settle_it.what: Confirmation that after the latest MAIM firmware/GUI and mag calibration the AHRS state and Trickster GPS/INS feed were normal

reasoning: The software engineer on the duplicate ticket found the customer did not have the correct MAIM firmware and GUI and that current firmware detects whether an AHRS is present and configures itself. That fits the AHRS X state on an Advanced Nav aircraft, but there is no record that the problem cleared after the update.
notes: FS2-3635 is marked as a duplicate of this ticket and holds the only engineering answer.

event: TIQUILA crews flying VXE-538 and VXE-553 reported that the Eagle mission simulator could not simulate the full mission, ELZ or lost link orbits in flight and gave false insufficient endurance warnings, with faults increasing with range.
failure_mode: simulator only simulates elements ahead on the current path in flight, omits ELZ and lost comms orbits, reports wrong endurance
contributing: faults reported to grow with flight duration and distance from the GCS

evidence.quote: The system would only simulate the full mission including ELZ and lost comms orbits while the aircraft was on the ground.
When simulation was applied during flight the system incorrectly reported insufficient endurance to complete the mission despite adequate battery power being available.
Simulation functions became less dependable the further the aircraft was from the Ground Control Station.
Known issues with current sim. Customer is notified of known issues. CA to replace with new sim.

team_view_in_comments: Known issues with current sim. Customer is notified of known issues. CA to replace with new sim.

would_settle_it.what: GCS and link data to check whether the range related faults were link bandwidth or simulator logic

reasoning: The described behavior is a limitation of the current simulator: it works fully on the ground but in flight only simulates what lies ahead and miscalculates endurance. The team recorded these as known simulator issues to be fixed with a new simulator, which places the cause in ground software design, though no analysis of the range related faults is recorded.
notes: Title has typo VVE-538 for VXE-538. Several abnormalities on one ticket; the reported range related faults were not analyzed.

event: VXE-471 (MCWL, out of warranty) came in because it could not connect to the GCS; on power up it sparked, and a power short had burned the nose power harness, fuselage harness and avionics box.
component: 16-pin nose ODU connector / nose power harness
failure_mode: power short (pins 5 and 7) causing a surge that burned wiring and components from nose to avionics box
contributing: nosecone power harness had been modified by the customer (tiedown) and was found melted
customer known to use experimental payloads
cable tester was not in use when this vehicle was built; cables passed functional and Ironbird checks

evidence.quote: The only we could confirm is the 5 and 7 pin short
A severe power surge burned wires and components from nose to box.
I think the most likely location of the instigating short is in the 16pos nose ODU.
I think the customer was known to use experimental payloads
Spark upon power up. Showing power fluctuations. Pulled Nose cone off to test branch cable components and found modified and melted main power harness.
Modifications made- Tiedown for nosecone power Harness.

team_view_in_comments: I think the most likely location of the instigating short is in the 16pos nose ODU.

would_settle_it.what: Burn pattern at the 16-pin nose ODU and the modified power harness to locate the first short (RMA-745 attachments 471Nose.jpg, 471Nose.1.jpg, 471Nose.2.jpg)
Section the 16-pin nose ODU and modified harness to confirm where the 5 to 7 pin short started

attachments_read: 31767_Old Fuse Power Harness and old rf cables.pdf.md
46637_ManTech Advanced Sys Int, Inc. - RMA VXE-453,.pdf.md
reasoning: The cable tester confirmed a pin 5 to pin 7 short, and the damage runs from the nose to the avionics box, consistent with a power short near the nose. Engineering judged the most likely start point to be the 16-pin nose ODU, and the RMA report found the nose power harness had been modified and melted. Root cause work was stopped because the aircraft was out of warranty, so the start point and whether the customer modification caused it remain unconfirmed.
notes: Ticket canceled; the team chose to replace damaged parts without RCCA. Several RMA-745 PDFs are scans with no text. The ManTech quote covers seven MCWL aircraft; only the VXE-471 page is relevant.

event: MOLSON reported E140 gimbals on two aircraft lost GPS in flight and could not regain it after power cycling, so Look Here and slew to GPS location did not work; HSV saw the same on VXE 734 with gimbal 6421 after a gimbal power cycle.
failure_mode: gimbal GNSS not reacquiring (VN board not initializing) after gimbal power cycle
contributing: gimbal GPS, Look Here and laser checks were skipped in ground checkout of customer cables
customer cables replaced many times over six weeks; possible GPS cable or connector damage
reacquisition after in-air power cycle often took several minutes

evidence.quote: I have reviewed the details of this incident and determined it is a result of intermittently degraded environmental conditions.
GPS in the area on other devices was not effected. Only the gimbal
Outdoors. Non-degraded environment. 10 minutes.
After this action, GPS functionality was lost and has not yet been restored.
those last two images likely indicate the VN board is not initializing.
In most instances, after power cycling in the air, the GPS would take several minutes to reacquire signal.

team_root_cause: Root cause is determined to be intermittently degraded environmental conditions.
disagreement: The team closed this as degraded GPS environment, but the customer said "GPS in the area on other devices was not effected. Only the gimbal" and tested "Outdoors. Non-degraded environment. 10 minutes." The linked HSV case lost gimbal GPS right after a power cycle, and an engineer read the diagnostics as "the VN board is not initializing", which points at the gimbal GNSS rather than the environment.

would_settle_it.what: E140 GPS diagnostic error window (PLD-54) to see whether the GNSS board reported an initialization fault
Aircraft GPS satellites, CNo and PDOP at the time the gimbal lost GPS, to confirm or rule out a degraded environment
Test the returned gimbal GNSS, antenna and GPS cable that never reconnected

reasoning: The loss of GPS was seen only on the gimbal while other GPS devices nearby worked, and the gimbal stayed without GPS for hours and across power cycles, which an environment issue does not explain well. The HSV case lost GPS right after a gimbal power cycle with diagnostics read as the VN board not initializing. No aircraft GPS logs or returned hardware were analyzed, so the gimbal GNSS is the leading candidate, not a confirmed part.
notes: Two separate aircraft at MOLSON (tails not given) plus the internal HSV case on VXE 734 / gimbal 6421 (PLD-54). Team members were themselves split between environment and software.

event: FBI fuel cell aircraft VXE-378 had several flights on 10 and 11 Sep 2025 with GCS overheating faults from the fuel cell and an HLB that ran down; logs showed a reactor over-temperature fault and a fuel remaining reset after an in-air fuel cell restart.
component: first generation D450 fuel cell cathode blower
failure_mode: cathode blower at its speed limit (about 9,800 to 10,000) could not supply enough airflow, reactor over-temperature fault 19742
contributing: high ambient heat, aircraft sat on the ground, and high power demand
operator launched and climbed straight to 1200 ft, draining the HLB faster than the fuel cell could recharge it
XCOMM/GCS bug resets fuel burned count on fuel cell restart (FS2-3497)

evidence.quote: This was the result of insufficient blower capacity in the first generation of fuel cells.
Their Cathode blowers typically capped out at around 9,800-10,000 which I can see from the data.
Cody is correct that the “depletion” of the HLB is related to the rapid ascent and insufficient time for the fuel cell to rebound.
Regarding reported ‘inability’ to charge HLB, it appears for this flight, operator launched aircraft and went immediately to 1200ft resulting in depletion of battery.
The XComm resets 'gburn_accum' to 0 during starts instead of only on initialization.

team_view_in_comments: This was the result of insufficient blower capacity in the first generation of fuel cells.
reasoning: The fuel cell engineer read the flight data and found the cathode blower pinned at its maximum speed while reactor temperature rose to the over-temperature fault, which names the blower capacity of the Gen 1 D450 as the cause. The HLB running down was shown in the data to be the high power climb outrunning the fuel cell, an operator profile issue rather than a charging fault. The fuel remaining jump is a known software bug tracked on FS2-3497.
notes: Three issues on one ticket: overheat (main), HLB depletion (operator climb), fuel remaining reset (software bug FS2-3497). Fault code written as 19472 by one engineer and 19742 by another. Vehicle Configuration field says Battery though the event is a fuel cell flight. Logs and images are listed only.

event: During a 1 h 15 min TIQUILA flight of VXE-555 the GCS Go To tool would not enter crosshair mode or select mission elements, so the crew let the aircraft finish its orbit and land on its mission.
failure_mode: Go To button accepted but active map tool apparently switched away immediately, so no Go To command could be sent
contributing: GCS debug and event logs lacked the detail to trace the map tool change; extra logging added for GCS 6.6.0

evidence.quote: The only conceivable root cause is something else in the system immediately switching the active map tool to something else.
The active map tool has timeout logic that is susceptible to a bad calculation after system uptime of 49.7 days.
I ruled this out via the logs, and it also would’ve only failed once every 49.7 days.
We don’t have enough information in GCS debug/event logs to investigate further.

team_root_cause: Possible: GetTickCount() rollover after 49.7 days system uptime causing map tool continuous timeout.
disagreement: The Root Cause field names a GetTickCount() rollover after 49.7 days of uptime, but the engineer who traced the code wrote "I ruled this out via the logs, and it also would’ve only failed once every 49.7 days." and concluded only that something switched the active map tool away. The evidence therefore narrows the fault to the GCS map tool handling without confirming the rollover.

would_settle_it.what: GCS event and debug logs around the failed Go To attempts, to see what changed the active map tool
Added map tool logging from any repeat occurrence

reasoning: The GCS checks for enabling Go To all passed, so the failure lies in the GCS map tool being replaced right after selection. The aircraft XCOMM log of the 18 Sep flight shows Go To commands earlier in the flight and none after the last mission upload at 13:06 until landing, which fits commands never leaving the GCS. The engineer ruled out the uptime rollover named in the Root Cause field and found no other cause in the logs.
notes: Large XCOMM and VTOL text logs (XC250923, VT250922, about 450 KB each) were read by searching for faults, mode changes, GoTo, mission, link and landing lines, skipping TRACE task dumps. CSV summaries hold headers only. The flight matching the report appears in XC250923 (startup 2025/09/18, launch 12:02, landing 13:15).
